newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Australia understands amnesty for rebel leader.
newsitem.headline: Australia understands amnesty for rebel leader.

text.p: Australia regrets but understands Cambodia's decision to grant an amnesty to dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary, a visiting member of the administration said on Monday.

But Andrew Thompson, a Liberal Party MP and parliamentary foreign affairs secretary, said Canberra would never accept amnesty for the murderers of Australians David Wilson and Kellie Wilkinson in 1994.

Thompson, the most senior member of Prime Minister John Howard's government to visit Cambodia, said the September 14 royal pardon of Ieng Sary, foreign minister during the brutal 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime of Pol Pot, was aimed at bringing peace to the country.
"We regretted very much the fact that he was given an amnesty but we recognise in a terrible way that it was a necessary evil," he told a meeting of the Australian business community.

In 1979 Ieng Sary was sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the genocide of more than one million people during the Khmer Rouge rule. He broke with hardliners loyal to Pol Pot in August and forged a ceasefire with the government.
But Ieng Sary said the government must clarify his legal status before peace talks could make further progress.
However, Thompson said no flexibility would be shown in the case of Wilson and Wilkinson, adding Australia would "reject the notion of amnesties being given to the murderers of those two people".

Chhouk Rin, commander of Khmer Rouge guerrillas who snatched Wilson and two others from a train in southern Cambodia, defected to the government before the bodies of the hostages were found and has said his commander, Nuon Paet, was responsible for their deaths.

Nuon Paet is still on the run while Chhouk Rin is a colonel in the royal armed forces. Last year a court sentenced a Khmer Rouge soldier to 15 years imprisonment for his role in the killing of Wilkinson and two British nationals, but the ringleaders remain free.
Thompson, who arrived on Friday for talks on political, economic and aid issues, stressed that his government would "continue vigorously to support the development of this country".
He announced shortly after arriving in the capital that Canberra would give A$575,000 (US$448,500) in aid for the victims of flooding along the Mekong River.
